However, designing non-truthful auctions remains challenging because bidders' equilibrium strategies depend on the auction mechanism and thus evolve as the mechanism is optimized.

radar.title: At What Cost? (In)efficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions
radar.summary: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions. We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation. We first show that the standard first-price procurement auction has no bounded PoA guarantee. We construct equilibria in which every bidder is indifferent between all bids in a common interval, so that bids can be arbitrarily large, and the PoA is unbounded. If costs lie in an interval $[\underline c,\bar c]$ but bids are not restricted, the PoA equals the trivial ratio $\bar c/\underline c$. We hence study ways to restore a finite guarantee, first by characterizing the PoA when bids lie in $[\underline c,\bar c]$, which leads to the tight bound $1 + \frac1{e^2}(\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}-1)$. Alternatively, we introduce the notion of a phantom bidder: the auctioneer accepts the lowest bid only if it does not exceed a phantom bid, drawn independently of the costs, and otherwise buys from an outside option at cost $\bar c$. We show that a simple fixed phantom bid, i.e., a deterministic cap, gives PoA $=\frac1e\sqrt {\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}+O(1)$. We further show that no phantom mechanism whose construction depends only on the cost interval, under a mild regularity condition, whatever distribution it uses and whatever it reveals about the phantom bid before bidding, can improve on the $\sqrt{\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}$ dependence.
radar.summary_short: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions. We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation.

radar.title: Equity Equilibrium for Cooperative Games
Online LLM Inference Routing for Multi-Agent Systems under Long-Term Budget and Layered Privacy Constraints
radar.summary: Abstract The Cloud-Edge-End (CEE) collaborative architecture has become a key paradigm for deploying highly intelligent multi-agent systems with low latency and high energy efficiency. Existing studies on efficient task offloading in CEE, however, either overlook long-term financial budget constraints from commercial API token usage and edge computing leasing, or inadequately handle layered information-sharing and privacy restrictions in decentralized autonomous agents. This paper investigates online inference routing to minimize the computational and communication overhead of large language model (LLM) workloads under long-term budget constraints, agent intent-sharing limitations, and un-known future prompt lengths. We propose a budget-aware online optimization framework that uses Lyapunov optimization to decouple long-term financial constraints, and show that the decoupled problem forms a generalized ordinal potential game. To address heterogeneous information-sharing restrictions, we design an adaptive best response algorithm for cooperative environments with shared decision information, and a multi-agent distributed routing algorithm for limited-information environments, enabling efficient offloading without inter-agent intent sharing. Theoretical analysis provides conditional performance and queue-length bounds and establishes finite convergence of the per-slot solvers. Simulations on distributed inference testbeds show that our scheme reduces the inference overhead of heterogeneous agentic tasks while achieving a favorable trade-off between performance and actual token expenditure.
radar.summary_short: Abstract The Cloud-Edge-End (CEE) collaborative architecture has become a key paradigm for deploying highly intelligent multi-agent systems with low latency and high energy efficiency.

radar.title: An Axiomatic Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Open multi-agent systems, where only a subset of agents are controllable, are central to real-world domains such as smart grids, yet lack a principled foundation for reinforcement learning algorithm design. We study this setting through n-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT), a recent framework for learning in open multi-agent environments. We propose an axiomatic framework that derives value function learning from the Shapley axioms (Efficiency, Symmetry and Linearity), treating them as structural constraints rather than heuristic design choices. This formulation builds on a novel NAHT decomposition, which characterises the fundamental difference between open and fully controllable multi-agent systems, and establishes a cooperative game-theoretic foundation for learning. We further show that enforcing these axioms on learning individual value functions recovers the Shapley value for Dec-POMDPs, providing a principled bridge between reinforcement learning and classical cooperative game theory. Building on this framework, we introduce Shapley Machines and Banzhaf Machines, two generic algorithmic templates that can be instantiated with standard reinforcement learning methods. When applied to strong base algorithms such as IPPO and POAM, our methods consistently improve learning efficiency and generalisation to unseen agent types and conventions across NAHT benchmark tasks. The code of experiments is published on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/axiomatic-rl-naht.
radar.summary_short: Open multi-agent systems, where only a subset of agents are controllable, are central to real-world domains such as smart grids, yet lack a principled foundation for reinforcement learning algorithm design.

Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model
radar.summary: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.

radar.title: Verification Allocation in Stylized LLM Agent Pipelines under Hidden Tool Degradation: A Discrete-Time Mean-Field Analysis
radar.summary: We study a stylized verification-allocation model for role-structured pipelines with binary inherited corruption and hidden tool degradation. Standard contraction arguments give serial and multi-role fixed points and a finite-population deviation bound under independence. When verification actions affect neither future errors nor observations, the belief-state choice is myopic. We characterize a two-action threshold under an explicit monotonicity condition and a restricted four-action interval and tail policy when generation rates are equal and only one check degrades. Synthetic experiments check these model-specific results and find counterexamples outside the restriction. This is conditional model analysis, not a general mean-field-game result or empirical evidence about deployed LLM systems.
radar.summary_short: We study a stylized verification-allocation model for role-structured pipelines with binary inherited corruption and hidden tool degradation. Standard contraction arguments give serial and multi-role fixed points and a finite-population deviation bound under independence.

radar.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Multi-agent systems of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across domains, introducing dynamics not captured by single-agent evaluations. Yet, existing work has mostly contrasted the behavior of a single agent with that of a collective of fixed size, leaving open a central question: How does group size shape dynamics? Here, we move beyond this dichotomy and systematically explore outcomes across the full range of group sizes. We focus on multi-agent misalignment, building on recent evidence that interacting LLMs playing a simple coordination game can generate collective biases absent in individual models. First, we show that collective bias is a deeper phenomenon than previously assessed: Interaction can amplify individual biases, introduce new ones, or override model-level preferences. Second, we demonstrate that group size affects the dynamics in a nonlinear way, revealing model-dependent dynamical regimes. Finally, we develop a mean-field analytical approach and show that, above a critical population size, simulations converge to deterministic predictions that expose the basins of attraction of competing equilibria. These findings establish group size as a key driver of multi-agent dynamics and highlight the need to consider population-level effects when deploying LLM-based systems at scale.

radar.title: In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?
radar.summary: When Learning About a Match Stalls the Market In many matching markets, participants must investigate whether a match is feasible. When inspection is costly, participants may delay investigating a potential match until both sides have effectively committed. Such caution can cause each side to wait for others to act, creating an “information deadlock.” In their article, “In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?” Immorlica, Kanoria, and Lu study this problem in random two-sided markets. They characterize how deadlock depends on the market balance, market connectivity, and the chance that inspections succeed. Using statistical physics tools, their analysis identifies phase transitions between deadlock-free and deadlocked markets. The findings offer design guidance: More choice is not always better; match rates are highest at the deadlock phase boundary; and parallel inspections and clearer participant differentiation can reduce the extent to which waiting chains stall the market.

radar.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
radar.summary: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. radar.title: Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
radar.summary: This monograph introduces discrete-time mean field games with finite state and action spaces, emphasizing optimization formulations and learning algorithms. Starting from Markov decision processes and finite-player stochastic games, it develops the notion of mean field Nash equilibrium, establishes existence and uniqueness results under suitable assumptions, and explains how mean field equilibria yield approximate equilibria in large finite-player games. Building on the linear programming formulation of Markov decision processes, occupation measures and primal-dual formulations connect equilibrium computation with mathematical optimization. The monograph presents fixed-point iterations, fictitious play, online mirror descent, and optimization-based methods, discussing their convergence properties and limitations. Numerical examples illustrate crowd motion, traffic routing, epidemic management, and the computation of multiple equilibria. It combines examples, theoretical results, and implementable algorithms, with bibliographic notes providing connections to the broader literature.

radar.title: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
radar.summary: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.

radar.title: INGENIERÍA ECONÓMICO-JURÍDICA, ACTUARIAL Y FINANCIERA DE SOCIEDADES POLICÉNTRICAS AUTÓNOMAS
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: PROGRAMA/TESIS DOCTORAL INDEPENDIENTE Proyecto de investigación fundacional Arquitectura científica propuesta INGENIERÍA ECONÓMICO-JURÍDICA, ACTUARIAL Y FINANCIERA DE SOCIEDADES POLICÉNTRICAS AUTÓNOMAS Fundamentos para la transición hacia órdenes sociales privados, voluntarios, criptográficamente verificables, mutuales, cooperativos, industriales y patrimonialmente descentralizados. Objeto central: Construcción de un marco científico integral para estudiar las condiciones económicas, jurídicas, actuariales, financieras, tecnológicas e institucionales que permitirían la transición desde sociedades organizadas mediante monopolios territoriales de autoridad hacia sociedades de coordinación policéntrica, contractual, privada y voluntaria. Portada e identificación académica Título principal: Fundamentos para la transición hacia órdenes sociales privados Subtítulo científico: Teoría de los polimonopolios endógenos multilocales Naturaleza independiente de la investigación: Tesis doctoral independiente Autoría: Fermín Ulaneo. Declaración de originalidad y trazabilidad documental: Susceptible de contrastación empírica. 2. Resumen ejecutivo de la investigación 2.1. Resumen general La investigación propone desarrollar una teoría integral de organización económica y jurídica basada en la coordinación voluntaria de individuos, empresas, propietarios, inventores, instituciones mutuales, organizaciones cooperativas y redes privadas de prestación de servicios. El objeto fundamental consiste en identificar, formalizar y evaluar las condiciones necesarias para constituir órdenes sociales capaces de coordinar producción, intercambio, financiación, protección patrimonial, resolución de conflictos, aseguramiento de riesgos, generación monetaria privada y provisión de infraestructuras sin depender estructuralmente de una autoridad territorial monopolística. La propuesta introduce una arquitectura institucional basada en siete elementos fundamentales: Policentrismo institucional: coexistencia de múltiples centros autónomos de decisión, contratación, financiación y prestación de servicios. Polimonopolios endógenos multilocales: organizaciones privadas que alcanzan posiciones de exclusividad económica mediante capacidades productivas, reputacionales, tecnológicas, contractuales y de coordinación, cuya continuidad depende de la aceptación voluntaria y de su capacidad para conservar clientes, capital y colaboradores. Mutualismo actuarial: agrupaciones voluntarias de personas y empresas para compartir riesgos mediante mecanismos de aseguramiento, reservas, reaseguro y distribución contractual de pérdidas. Propiedad productiva descentralizada: estructuras de propiedad, inversión, sucesión y capitalización capaces de multiplicar unidades productivas independientes. Infraestructuras monetarias y financieras privadas: sistemas de intercambio, liquidación, crédito, ahorro y financiación basados en reglas verificables y mecanismos competitivos. Resolución policéntrica de conflictos: instituciones especializadas en arbitraje, mediación, adjudicación y ejecución contractual. Juegos evolutivos dinámicos endógenos volitivos: una nueva arquitectura de análisis de decisiones estratégicas en la que los agentes pueden modificar preferencias, capacidades, compromisos, alianzas, reglas y estructuras de cooperación a lo largo del tiempo. La tesis no presupone que toda interacción económica sea necesariamente beneficiosa para todos los participantes. Investiga, por el contrario, bajo qué condiciones pueden transformarse conflictos distributivos, externalidades, incertidumbres y problemas de coordinación en procesos de creación conjunta de valor. El resultado esperado es una teoría institucional susceptible de formalización matemática, evaluación actuarial, análisis financiero, contrastación histórica y experimentación mediante simulaciones computacionales. 2.2. Abstract The research develops an interdisciplinary framework for the economic, legal, actuarial and financial foundations of polycentric voluntary societies. Its central objective is to investigate the institutional, technological and contractual conditions under which decentralized private organizations can provide economic coordination, insurance, monetary services, capital allocation, dispute resolution and productive infrastructure without relying on territorially monopolistic political authority. The proposed framework introduces endogenous multilocal poly-monopolies, voluntary mutual insurance architectures, decentralized productive ownership, private financial infrastructures, contractual governance and endogenous volitional evolutionary game theory. The research combines institutional economics, contract theory, mechanism design, actuarial mathematics, financial economics, cryptographic verification, evolutionary dynamics and industrial organization. Its principal scientific contribution is intended to be a formal and empirically testable architecture explaining how voluntary institutions emerge, compete, cooperate, adapt and reproduce across multiple geographical and technological environments. 2.3. Problema científico central ¿Cómo diseñar, financiar, asegurar, gobernar y reproducir sistemas sociales complejos en los que las funciones actualmente concentradas en instituciones territoriales monopolísticas puedan ser desarrolladas por redes autónomas, privadas, mutuales, cooperativas y contractuales? 2.4. Solución científica propuesta Desarrollar una arquitectura institucional multicapa que permita: Sustitución funcional progresiva de estructuras monopolísticas. Creación de organizaciones privadas de gobernanza. Desarrollo de sistemas monetarios competitivos. Provisión privada de servicios de protección, seguridad y justicia. Financiación industrial y tecnológica descentralizada. Aseguramiento mutual de riesgos sistémicos. Protección de derechos patrimoniales. Coordinación contractual entre jurisdicciones voluntarias. Expansión de las capacidades productivas humanas. Reducción de los costes de conflicto y cooperación. 2.5. Resultados y aportaciones esperadas La investigación aspira a producir: Una teoría económica de los polimonopolios endógenos. Una teoría actuarial de las sociedades mutuales autónomas. Una arquitectura jurídica de órdenes contractuales policéntricos. Un modelo financiero de capitalización institucional privada. Una teoría de transición monetaria sin banca central. Una teoría de transición institucional sin Estado. Una teoría evolutiva de cooperación y creación conjunta de valor. Un modelo cuantitativo de sostenibilidad intergeneracional. 3. Introducción general 3.1. Planteamiento del problema Las sociedades industriales contemporáneas concentran importantes funciones de coordinación económica, jurídica, monetaria, financiera y territorial en instituciones dotadas de facultades exclusivas. La investigación parte de una pregunta diferente: ¿Es posible desarrollar arquitecturas institucionales alternativas capaces de proporcionar esas mismas funciones, o funciones superiores, mediante organizaciones autónomas que compitan, cooperen, se especialicen y se coordinen voluntariamente? Esta pregunta requiere superar el tratamiento exclusivamente ideológico de la organización social. No basta con proponer la desaparición de una institución. Es necesario determinar: Qué funciones desempeña. Qué problemas resuelve. Qué incentivos sostienen su funcionamiento. Qué costes genera. Qué instituciones alternativas podrían asumir sus funciones. Qué mecanismos impedirían su captura. Cómo se financiarían. Cómo se asegurarían sus obligaciones. Cómo se resolverían los conflictos entre ellas. Cómo se produciría la transición sin provocar discontinuidades sistémicas. Por tanto, la abolición institucional, cuando sea objeto de la investigación, deberá estudiarse como un problema de sustitución funcional, no como una simple eliminación administrativa. 3.2. La unidad fundamental de análisis Se propone sustituir el análisis centrado exclusivamente en Estados, mercados nacionales y empresas individuales por una unidad institucional más amplia: La red autónoma de coordinación económico-jurídica. Esta unidad puede integrar: Individuos. Familias. Empresas. Cooperativas. Mutualidades. Aseguradoras. Organizaciones arbitrales. Redes de seguridad. Fondos de inversión. Instituciones monetarias. Plataformas tecnológicas. Organizaciones industriales. Redes de propietarios. Sistemas privados de acreditación y certificación. Cada organización constituye un agente institucional con recursos, capacidades, compromisos, derechos, obligaciones y mecanismos propios de adaptación. 3.3. Justificación de la investigación La investigación se justifica por la necesidad de integrar disciplinas que habitualmente estudian separadamente los problemas de organización social. Disciplina

radar.title: DisC: Incentive Design for Green, Robust, and Fair Client Self-Participation in OTA Federated Learning
radar.summary: Over-the-Air Federated Learning (OTA-FL) improves communication efficiency by exploiting waveform superposition over wireless Multiple-Access Channels (MAC). However, client heterogeneity, fading, energy constraints, and participation imbalance can degrade both fairness and aggregation accuracy. Existing Pareto-oriented fair OTA-FL schemes may still suffer from large aggregation distortion when highly weighted clients experience poor channel conditions. This paper proposes DisC, a game-theoretic distributed client selection framework for fairness-aware, channel-aware, and energy-efficient OTA-FL. Each client selects its participation level by maximizing a utility that captures Pareto fairness importance, learning relevance, OTA distortion, energy consumption, and delay. We show that DisC admits a Nash equilibrium and can be formulated as an exact potential game, where stable equilibria correspond to locally optimal OTA-FL operating points. DisC therefore offers a distributed, incentive-compatible alternative to centralized client selection under wireless and resource constraints.

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can be overly conservative and fail to use observations about the active attack regime. We propose posterior-conditioned MARL, a context-aware framework formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. Experiments on the Cyber Autonomy Gym for Experimentation (CybORG) CAGE-4 cyber operations testbed show improved mission reward and adaptability, particularly under mixed and switching attack conditions, compared with domain-randomized, worst-case robust, and hierarchical defense baselines.

radar.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.
